demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making any plans for the future
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
The world is a dangerous place
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Perpetrator' cues are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one; this wording implies an assaultive interpersonal trauma rather than bereavement-related PTSD.

issues.item: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: 'Safe seat seeking' fits fear of immediate interpersonal attack or entrapment more than traumatic bereavement. In combination with startle/hypervigilance, it shifts the profile toward assault-type threat rather than loss-related PTSD, with no supporting trauma-specific content elsewhere.

vignette: Rahul, a 20-year-old South Asian male and writer, has experienced profound emotional distress following the unexpected death of his older brother. The tragic event occurred about eight months ago when Rahul’s brother was struck by a car while walking home from work late one night. Despite Rahul not witnessing the accident himself, the sudden and senseless loss has left him grappling with intense feelings of grief and fear. Rahul had always been close to his brother, often turning to him for advice and support. His brother's death shattered Rahul’s belief that the world was a safe place where good things happened to good people. Since then, he has found it nearly impossible to relax even when in the safety of his own home. Ordinary sounds like the creaking of floorboards or a doorbell can make him jump and feel on edge. Rahul's sleep has been severely disrupted as well. He finds himself constantly waking up during the night with his heart racing, unable to shake off the sense that something terrible could happen at any moment. These nights are often punctuated by flashbacks of the last time he saw his brother alive—a conversation they had over a casual dinner. In an attempt to cope with his overwhelming grief and anxiety, Rahul has begun avoiding making any future plans. The idea of setting goals or looking ahead feels too painful; it reminds him that life continues without his brother. He often finds himself asking friends and family for reassurance, seeking comfort in their words that everything will be okay. However, the more he seeks this reassurance, the less grounded and secure he feels. Rahul’s work as a writer has also been affected by these changes. His writing desk, once a sanctuary of creativity and solace, now seems to mock him with reminders of his brother. The typewriter they used together in their shared room becomes a trigger that evokes intense sadness and anxiety. Rahul avoids the room altogether, often working in cafes or parks where he feels somewhat anonymous. His relationships have also suffered as a result of these changes. Friends and family have noticed his growing isolation and increasing irritability. They’ve tried to offer support, but their attempts often fall short of what Rahul needs. He has come to believe that the world is inherently dangerous and that happiness is now unattainable for him. The breaking point came last week when Rahul received a manuscript from an old friend asking him to read it over before publication. The request dredged up memories of times they had spent together, laughing and sharing stories. This time, however, instead of feeling joy, he was overwhelmed with grief and panic, feeling that even the simplest tasks were too much. What frightens Rahul most is the fear of never finding happiness again and living in a constant state of heightened alertness. He has begun to see how his avoidance behaviors are isolating him further from those who care about him and from activities he once enjoyed. Despite this awareness, he feels helpless to change his course without professional help. Rahul’s most fervent hope is that with the right support, he can learn to navigate these intense emotions and rediscover some semblance of peace and happiness in his life. He believes that understanding how his thoughts and behaviors are interconnected might help him regain a sense of control over his experiences.
